work.title: Sermo ad Caesariensis Ecclesiae Plebem

paragraphs.text: You know how joyfully we welcome the eagerness of your charity. We exult in the Lord our God, of whom the apostle says: "For he is our peace, who has made both one." So we give thanks to that same Lord and Saviour of ours, Jesus Christ, who has granted us, even before we have the consent of our brother Emeritus, to learn already how much he loves unity. But hear the opening words God willed us to hear from his own mouth. As soon as he entered this church, standing in the place where we first began our conversation with him, by the inspiration of the Lord, who both instructs the heart and governs the tongue, he said to us: "I cannot refuse to want what you want, but I can want what I want." See what he has promised, he who said he cannot refuse to want what we want. For if he cannot refuse to want what we want, he knows what we want; and we want what you want too, and all of us want what God wants. What the Lord wants is no secret. For the testament is read of him who made us his co-heirs, and in it these words are recited: "My peace I give you, my peace I leave you." So, whether soon or late, he cannot refuse to want what we want. But his second statement causes us some delay: "I can want what I want." For this is what he said: "I cannot refuse to want what you want, but I can want what I want." He can want what he wants, but he cannot refuse to want what we want. What he says he can do, we see him doing. For at present he wants what he wants, and what he wants at present God does not want. What does he want at present? To be at odds with the Catholic Church, to remain still in the communion of the party of Donatus, to remain still in schism, to remain still among those who say: "I belong to Paul, I to Apollos, I to Cephas." But God does not want this, for the apostle rebukes it: "Is Christ divided?" So he can want what he wants, but only for a time, only for the hour of embarrassment; he can want what he wants, but not by the reckoning of wisdom. At present this is what he wants, and he can want what he wants. But since he cannot refuse to want what we want, let him quickly stop wanting what he wants and do what we want. So, brothers, do not let a little delay trouble you while he wants what he wants; rather pray that he will do what he has promised, so that he cannot refuse to want what we want. — And everyone shouted: "Either here or nowhere!" — You who have declared your hearts with your voices, help us with your prayers as well. The Lord, who commands unity, is able to change a will for the better. As for what your charity shouted, "Either here or nowhere," we recognize in it the voice of your charity toward him, and we love it. This is not something we are thinking of now for the first time; we always think of it, always long for it. The same is the mind, and this is especially necessary, of our brother and fellow bishop Deuterius, your bishop. We have long known his mind. He poured out prayers to the Lord with us on this matter in the council where we promised and offered this to those who are outside. Our signatures on this matter are already on record. For we never cherish our own rank so much that we begrudge unity. Let us be lesser in rank, so long as we are greater in love. We know how weakness must be coaxed, so that unity may be achieved.

Nor do we say this, brothers, as though those who remain in schism have any hope before the Lord. For many people argue, understanding little of what they are saying, and say: "If they are schismatics, if they are heretics, why are they received like this?" Listen, my brothers. If we received them as they are, we would already have received this brother of ours, Emeritus, whether good or bad, but still a brother. I call him that because he too knows that it was said to us through the prophet, as we also told them at the conference: "Say 'You are our brothers' to those who hate you." They hate us; we trust that their hatred will come to an end. Yet as long as he hates, he hears himself called "brother." Until the hatred ends, the name will stand as a testimony. So we do not receive them as they are, far be it from us, for they are heretics; but we receive Catholics: they are changed, and they are received. Yet because of the evil they have, we cannot attack in them the good things we recognize. The evil of dissension, of schism, of heresy is their own evil; but the good things we recognize in them are not their own. They have our Lord's good things, the Church's good things. Baptism is not theirs but Christ's. The invocation of the name of God over their heads when bishops are ordained is God's invocation, not Donatus's. I would not receive a man as bishop if, when he was ordained, Donatus was invoked over his head. In a soldier who strays and deserts, the crime belongs to the deserter, but the mark belongs not to the deserter but to the emperor. Our brother, however, did not desert, since he has never yet been with us; rather, the deserter's error was born in him when he was marked by a deserter. The one who first made the schism, who separated himself from the Catholic Church, was a deserter, together with those he drew along with him. The rest were marked by deserters, yet not with the deserter's mark but with the emperor's, for the deserter did not imprint a mark of his own. What do I mean by saying the deserter did not imprint his own mark? Donatus did not baptize in the name of Donatus. If Donatus, when he made the schism, had baptized in the name of Donatus, he would have imprinted the deserter's mark. Then, when I called men to unity, if I found the deserter's mark, I would root it out, erase it, abolish it, throw it away; I would not approve it, I would reject it, anathematize it, condemn it. But as it is, the deserter himself imprinted the mark of his emperor. Our God and Lord Jesus Christ seeks out the deserter and wipes out the crime of error, but he does not root out his own mark. When I come to my brother and gather in my straying brother, I look to the faith in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. That is the mark of my emperor. Concerning this mark he gave a command to his soldiers, or rather his companions, that they should imprint it on those they were gathering into his camp, saying: "Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Because Paul knew that this mark had been ordained by the Lord to be imprinted on all believers, he was alarmed at those who wanted to belong to Paul, and he said to them: "Was Paul crucified for you? Why do you want to be mine, and not rather my Lord's? Why do you want to be mine, and not rather his whose I am? Recognize, take note of your mark: were you baptized in the name of Paul?" So we gather them in, but in such a way that those we do not gather in may not flatter themselves. Let them too be gathered in, and not be puffed up; let them come, and they will be received. We do not hate in them what is God's, nor do we hate them, because they are God's and what they have is God's. They are God's because they are human beings, and every human being is God's creature; it is God's that they have the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The baptism of the Trinity is God's, the gospel they have is God's, the faith they have is God's.

"Then what do they lack," someone says to me, "if they have these things? You say they have Christ's baptism?" I do. "You say they have the faith of Christ?" I do. "If they have these things, then, what do they lack?" What is baptism? A sacrament. Hear the apostle: "If I know all sacraments." It is a great thing to know all the sacraments of God; however many sacraments we may know, who knows all the sacraments of God? What does the apostle say? "If I know all sacraments, if I have all prophecy"; add further: "and all knowledge." ("But you were speaking about faith.") Hear further: "if I have all faith." It is hard to have all faith, just as it is hard to know all sacraments. And what is it he says? "All faith, so that I can move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing." Pay attention, brothers, pay attention, I beg you, to the apostle's words, and see why we seek our brothers with such labours and dangers. It is charity that seeks them, from our hearts. "For the sake of my brothers and my neighbours," says the psalm, "I spoke peace concerning you," speaking to holy Jerusalem. See, then, my brothers, what the apostle said: "If I have all sacraments, all knowledge, prophecy, faith" (what kind of faith?) "so that I can move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing." He did not say, "All those things are nothing," but: "If I have not charity, I am nothing." For what madman would say that the sacraments of God are nothing? What madman would say that prophecy is nothing, knowledge nothing, faith nothing? Those things are not nothing; but though they are great, if I who have great things have not charity, I am nothing. Those things are great, and I have great things, and yet I am nothing if I have not charity, through which the great things benefit me. For if I have not charity, those things can be in me, but they cannot benefit me.

So pay attention, brother, pay attention, I beg you. You say to me: "Why are you seeking me?" I answer: "Because you are my brother." You answer me and say: "If I am lost, why are you seeking me?" And I answer: "If you were not lost, I would not be seeking you." "Why are you seeking me?" you say to me. "If I am lost, why are you seeking me?" And I answer: "I am seeking you because you are lost." And why do I seek you, and for what reward? So that one day it may be said to me: "Your brother was dead and has come back to life; he was lost and has been found." You answer and say to me: "But I have the sacrament." You have it, I acknowledge it; that is why I am seeking you. You have added a great reason why I should seek you all the more diligently. For you are a sheep of my Lord's flock; you have strayed with his brand on you. That is why I seek you all the more, because you have that very brand. Why do we not possess one Church? We have one brand; why are we not in one fold? I am seeking you so that this sacrament may be a help to your salvation, not a testimony to your damnation. Do you not know that a deserter is condemned on account of the very mark for which a serving soldier is honoured? I am seeking you so that you may not perish with the brand on you. For it is a sign of salvation if you have salvation, if you have charity. Outside, this sign of salvation can be in you, but it cannot benefit you. Come, so that what you had may benefit you: not so that you may receive what you had, but so that what you had may begin to benefit you, and so that you may receive what you did not have. For you had the sign of peace, but you did not have peace itself. In that house, that is, in you, discord was living, and it was posting notices of peace on the threshold. I recognize the notices, but I am looking for the occupant. I read the notice of peace: baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. It is a notice of peace; I read it; I ask who lives there. I look at my brother; I recognize the notice of peace. I have it too; I want to come in. What does "I want to come in" mean? Accept me as a brother, so that we may pray to the Father together. "I will not pray with you." The notices are notices of peace, and discord opposes me? Clearly, with the Lord's help, I shall labour to throw out discord, the wrongful occupant, and to bring in peace as the lawful owner. When, then, I shut out discord and bring in peace, why should I take down the notices of peace? I say plainly to my Lord: "O Christ, who are our peace, who have made both one, make us one, so that we may rightly sing: 'See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity.' Bring in concord, drive out discord; bring yourself in to your own notices. Remain there yourself; let no other occupy the house and deceive by means of your notices. Change this opponent, you who in a single hour on the cross changed the thief."

And let us certainly see what you have. "I have the sacrament," you say, "I have baptism." If I say to you, "Prove it," you show me what you received, you tell me what you confessed, you tell me what you hold. I acknowledge it, I do not change it, I do not blow on it as though to exorcize it; far be it from me, while I seek the salvation of the deserter, to do injury to the emperor. So you have proved to me that you have the sacrament; by setting out the sacrament you have proved to me that you have faith. Prove to me that you have charity: hold fast to unity. I do not want you to tell me, "I have charity": prove it. We have one Father: let us pray together. What do you say when you pray, I ask you? "Our Father, who art in heaven." Thanks be to God. Following the teaching of our Lord you have added: "who art in heaven." For each of us had his own father on earth; together we have found one in heaven. "Our Father, who art in heaven": you call upon him as Father. Our Father willed to have one bride. Since we worship one Father, then, why do we not acknowledge one mother? If you say you were born of another woman, then she bore you, even if from a bosom not her own. Not all of you could understand what I have said. We know that, through lawful wives, it came about that even those who were not born of the lawful wives were made sharers in the same inheritance. It was the wife's will that brought this about. Ishmael, it is true, was disinherited. Yet Sarah had borne him, even if from another's womb. Sarah had borne him by another's womb, by her own wish. For she herself said, "I want you to beget children for me by her," and so Abraham did. "For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does." Ishmael would have been a son if he had not been proud; it was as a proud man that Ishmael was disinherited. For the slave-woman raised her neck, so that it was said: "Cast out the slave-woman and her son, for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac." Do you want to know what peace can do, what concord can do, what humility can do, and what pride hinders? Pride disinherited Ishmael; but the sons of the slave-women by Jacob, since the lawful wives too wanted them to be born, we know were called into the one inheritance. All twelve patriarchs were counted together; difference of womb separated none of them from the others, because charity united them all. What does it matter, then, where you received baptism? "The baptism is mine," Sarah tells you; "the baptism is mine," Rachel tells you. Do not be proud; come to the inheritance, especially since that inheritance is not the land given to the sons of Jacob. Land was given to the children of Israel; the more people possessed it, the more cramped it became. Our inheritance is called peace; I read the testament: "My peace I give you, my peace I leave you." Let us hold together what cannot be divided. A multitude of owners does not make it cramped, however many come, as was promised: "So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the shore of the sea. In your seed all nations shall be blessed." And, it says in Revelation, "I saw many in white robes and holding palms, whom no one could number, coming from all nations." Let them come, let them hold fast to peace. Our possession does not become cramped; nothing makes it cramped except dissension alone. See, my brothers: it is our brother's dissension that makes us still suffer this cramping. Let him agree in peace, and there is room at once.

But what are we to do, except bear with our brother's weakness and not give up? We trust that this sweat of mine will bear fruit. The Lord our God, who willed that we should come to you, who commanded us to seek him, who has brought it about that for the present we have found him face to face, will, with the help of your prayers, enable us to find his heart, to rejoice in his concord, and to thank God for his salvation, which he cannot have except in the Catholic Church. Outside the Catholic Church he can have everything except salvation: he can have rank, he can have the sacraments, he can sing alleluia, he can answer amen, he can hold the gospel, he can have and preach faith in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; but nowhere except in the Catholic Church will he be able to find salvation. For all those things pass away, my brothers. At present he thinks he will be great among his own people if he does not agree and is called a martyr of the party of Donatus. Far from it! In the name of the Lord, may this vanity be taken from his heart. He knows it too, he reads it too: "If I hand over my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing." I do not merely say that if he boasts of having suffered some injuries for the party of Donatus, or some earthly losses, it profits him nothing. I say more: suppose he were to suffer outside at the hands of an enemy of Christ, not his Catholic brother seeking his salvation, but an enemy of Christ; suppose that outside, apart from the Church of Christ, an enemy of Christ said to him, "Offer incense to idols, worship my gods," and he refused to worship and was killed by the enemy of Christ: he could shed his blood, but he could not receive the crown.

They themselves know how, when they were at our conference held at Carthage, they admitted that their forebears persecuted Bishop Caecilian. It was then that, falling out with the Catholic Church, they made the schism. Their forebears persecuted him; that is, the first founders of the party of Donatus persecuted Caecilian. By their persecution they brought him all the way to the emperor's judgment; they sent the emperor charges against him which were not true. The emperor ordered the case to be heard. It was heard before bishops, the charges were found to be false, and Caecilian was acquitted. Nor did they stop persecuting him, but petitioned the emperor again and again, until in the end they made him judge of the case, and he heard the parties himself and examined the matter. The emperor examined it and judged Caecilian innocent. And when we put this to them, they argued with us and said that the emperor had condemned Caecilian to exile. That is false. But see what they said: that through the persecution of their forebears Caecilian was brought before the emperor and sent into exile. We have read the official record; these are his own statements, and his signature, set to his own words, is on file. Pay attention, I beg you, and judge our case now. Certainly their forebears persecuted Caecilian, certainly they brought him before the emperor, certainly they got him condemned. I will not say that he was not condemned, I will not say that he was pronounced innocent; let it be as they say. When they were persecuting him, when they got him condemned, what was Caecilian then? When he was suffering persecution at the hands of their forebears, what was he? Tell me: what was he? Was he a Christian? Was he a Catholic? Or what was he? They do not say, "He was not a Catholic," but "He was a criminal." So criminals can suffer persecution at the hands of saints. Let us accept this completely: Caecilian, who was suffering persecution, was a criminal. I do not say they were lying, only that they were mistaken; but let us go so far as to agree with them: "He was a criminal." Those who were doing it, what were they? Choose whichever you like. If they were wicked, leave the wicked and come to us; but if they were holy, then it can happen that saints persecute an unjust man. Do not be angry with us if we persecute; do not say, "You who persecute are unjust." For you have already shown that it can happen that the just persecute the unjust. Can it happen or not? Tell me one of the two. If it cannot happen, why did your people persecute Caecilian? But if it can happen, why are you surprised? Why do you praise the suffering and not show the cause? "Blessed," says the Lord, "are those who suffer persecution." Add "for righteousness' sake," and you have set apart robbers, set apart sorcerers, set apart adulterers, set apart the impious, set apart the sacrilegious, set apart heretics. Such people suffer persecution, but not for righteousness' sake.

And yet, what sort of persecution is our brother suffering, who has been brought to us? That persecution is all the more glorious; I openly profess it. Let anyone who wishes find fault with me: such persecution I profess. I read the psalm: "Whoever secretly slandered his neighbour, him I persecuted." If I rightly persecute one who secretly slanders his neighbour, do I not more rightly persecute one who publicly blasphemes the Church of God, when he says, "That is not the Church," when he says, "Ours is the Church, the one in our party," when he says, "She is a harlot"? Shall I not, then, persecute one who blasphemes the Church? I shall plainly persecute him, because I am a member of the Church; I shall plainly persecute him, because I am a son of the Church. I use the very voice of the Church; the Church herself says through me in the psalm: "I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail." Let them fail in evil, and advance in good. Brothers, do not think anything new has been done to our brother. When the party of Donatus held the upper hand at Constantina, Petilian seized a layman of ours, a catechumen born of Catholic parents. He used force on him against his will; he searched for him when he fled, found him in hiding, dragged him out in terror, baptized him trembling, ordained him unwilling. See what violence he did to one of ours! He dragged him off to death; shall we not draw ours to salvation?

I have said this to your charity because of what you said: "Either here or nowhere." For we want this too: "here, here," but in peace; "here, here," but in unity; "here, here," but in the fellowship of charity. Then "here" is good. For if not so, "nowhere" is better than "here." But may the Lord grant that it be "here" rather than "nowhere." If not "here," God forbid that it should not be somewhere else; God forbid. Here or elsewhere. You have heard; he has heard. What God has worked in his mind, God knows. For we strike the ear from outside; he knows how to speak within, he preaches peace within and never ceases to preach it, if only he is heard. His mercy will be with us, helped by your prayers, so that our labour may bear fruit. Yet if he will not enter into communion today, we must not grow weary; we must press on as hard as we can, and even then we must not grow weary. We can postpone; we neither can nor should give up our insistence. He who led him here to us will be with us, to make us rejoice with him in unity with you and in his peace.
